title: Phishing Email Body Classifier
blurb: A trained model and a rule list, kept deliberately apart.

steps.say: This one judges the writing. Not the sender, not the links, not the headers, which other tools here already cover. Just whether the language reads like a phishing email.

Behind this is a real trained Naive Bayes classifier, ninety one percent accurate on a held out test set. That number is measured, and it is stated because ninety one percent also means roughly one in eleven wrong.
Likely phishing, with a probability rather than a yes or no. And underneath, the words that actually drove it. Those are pulled out of the model, not chosen afterwards to look convincing.

Separately, a small rule list looks for urgency phrasing and generic greetings. It found neither — and that is worth seeing. This email opens Hello and Urgent and says my dear, but the list holds exact phrases like urgent action required and dear customer, so it stays silent. A curated list is narrow by construction. That is exactly why it sits beside the model rather than folded into its score.
Now the other sample, an ordinary email.

Likely safe, at zero percent, and the contributing words are mostly green now, the ones that pull a message away from phishing. A couple still lean the other way and the model weighed them against the rest. This is the half people forget to check. A detector that only ever sees threats is not a detector, it is an alarm.

The rules are silent here too, and this time they are right. So across both emails the rules caught nothing and the model caught everything. That is the honest result, and it is the argument for showing you two signals separately rather than blending them into one number that hides which half did the work.
